The conference seeds the ground for the subsequent creation of the Non-Aligned Movement.

14-year-old Chicago teenager Emmett Till is lynched while vacationing in Money, Mississippi. Till was severely beaten, shot in the head, and thrown into the Tallahatchie River. His mother, Mamie Till-Bradley, immediately requests her son’s bloated, mutilated body be returned to Chicago and displayed in an open casket funeral at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ. She says, “I wanted the world to see what they did to my son.” Tens of thousands of people line up to view the body at the mortuary, and more than 50,000 mourners attend the funeral services days later.

Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., 26-year-old pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, is elected president of the Montgomery Improvement Association, which leads the year-long boycott against the city's racially segregated bus line.

FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover initiates COINTELPRO, the FBI's Counterintelligence Program, designed to "increase factionalism, cause disruption and win defections” inside the Communist Party U.S.A. The program is later expanded to include disruption of the Socialist Workers Party (1961), the Ku Klux Klan (1964), the Black Panther Party and the Nation of Islam (1967), and the entire New Left, including community and religious groups (1968).
Chinese Confession Program offers limited promise of legal status to undocumented Chinese who confess their status. However, many are not eligible for relief and were deported.
Punjabi Sikh Dalip Singh Saund, of the 29th District in Los Angeles, is the first Asian American elected to Congress.
Christian Evangelicals Henry and Bertha Holt establish the Holt Adoption Program to facilitate the adoption of Korean children by white American families.

Congress passes the Civil Rights Act of 1957, the first legislation protecting black rights since Reconstruction. The act establishes the Civil Rights section of the Justice Department and empowers federal prosecutors to obtain court injunctions against interference with the right to vote. It also creates the federal Civil Rights Commission with the authority to investigate discriminatory conditions and recommend corrective measures.

Pres. Dwight D. Eisenhower sends federal troops to Little Rock, Arkansas, to ensure the enforcement of a Federal court order to desegregate Central High School and to protect 9 black students from angry Whites.
The Southern Christian Leadership Conference forms in Atlanta, Georgia.

Cuban Revolution ends the Fulgencio Batista dictatorship when insurrection by guerrilla fighters led by Fidel Castro ousts Batista and forms a new, independent government. This begins decades of U.S. efforts to undermine the Cuban government through an embargo and covert actions.
Hawai’i and Alaska become U.S. states.
Four students from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College in Greensboro begin a sit-in at Woolworth's Drug Store to protest racially segregated counters.
NAACP official Ella Baker calls a conference at Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina, where 150 black and white students found the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).

Civil Rights Act, signed by Pres. Dwight D. Eisenhower, establishes federal inspection of local voter registration rolls and penalties for anyone who obstructs a citizen's attempt to register or to vote.

President Eisenhower, a retired five-star Army general, the man who led the allies on D-Day, talks about the danger of the collaboration between military forces and defense contractors in his farewell speech. Eisenhower was worried about the costs of an arms race with the Soviet Union; the resources it would divert from other areas, such as building hospitals and schools; and the corrupting force that a military-industrial alliance would have on government. He warns: "In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist."
Seven Blacks and four Whites leave Washington, D.C., for the Deep South in the first Freedom Ride.
Through the CIA, the United States begins recruiting and training residents of Laos (mostly Hmong) to help fight the Communist Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese in a “secret war.”
Western Samoa becomes the first Pacific Island nation to gain its independence from Western colonization. It would change its name to Samoa in 1997.

For 13 days, the Cuban Missile Crisis brings the United States and the Soviet Union closer to the threat of thermonuclear total war than at any other time in their history. Both nations pull back from the brink.
NAACP leader Medgar Evers is assassinated in Jackson, Mississippi.

George Wallace becomes Governor of Alabama by appealing to explicit racism and by courting support from white segregationists and the Ku Klux Klan. In his famous inaugural speech, he says, “…from this Cradle of the Confederacy, this very Heart of the Great Anglo-Saxon Southland… we sound the drum for freedom. …In the name of the greatest people that have ever trod this earth, I draw the line in the dust and toss the gauntlet before the feet of tyranny… and I say… segregation now… segregation tomorrow… segregation forever!” Later this year, Wallace announces his bid for presidency against Democratic incumbent John F. Kennedy.
The SCLC’s Birmingham Campaign, a series of lunch counter sit-ins, marches on City Hall and boycotts on downtown merchants to protest segregation laws in the city.
March on Washington. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivers his “I Have a Dream” speech to over 200,000 demonstrators demanding civil rights and equal opportunity.
U.S.-approved military coup overthrows Pres. Ngô Đình Diệmin of Vietnam.

Five Southern states give their electoral votes to GOP presidential candidate and staunch opponent of civil rights Barry Goldwater. This marks the start of the Republican takeover of the Deep South, also known as the Southern Strategy, by appealing to white resentment of black civil rights using racially coded language about states rights and crime. Goldwater says, “History shows us that nothing prepares the way for tyranny more than the failure of public officials to keep the streets safe from bullies and marauders. We Republicans seek a government that attends to its fiscal climate, encouraging a free and a competitive economy and enforcing law and order.”
SNCC organizes Mississippi Freedom Summer.

One black (James Earl Chaney) and two Jewish (Andrew Goodman and Michael “Mickey” Schwerner) civil rights workers with the Freedom Summer campaign are murdered in Neshoba County, Mississippi, by members of the local Ku Klux Klan. The Neshoba County Sheriff’s Office and the Philadelphia, Mississippi, Police Department are also involved.
The Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP) delegation, led by Fannie Lou Hamer, is denied seating at the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City in August.

Pres. Lyndon Johnson announces his Great Society program during his State of the Union address, a series of domestic programs promising to eliminate poverty and inequality in America. By the end of Johnson’s term, Congress would implement 226 of 252 his legislative requests, including the voting rights act, and Medicare and Medicaid, the 1965 immigration act.
Civil Rights Act bans discrimination in employment and all public accommodations, and establishes the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission (EEOC).
Pres. Lyndon Johnson signs the Economic Opportunity Act, initiating the federally sponsored War on Poverty. The act includes Head Start, Upward Bound, and Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA).

Watts Rebellion. 30,000 protest for 5 days in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Watts, resulting from frequent police violence and racial discrimination against blacks in housing, education, employment, and political life. The uprising ends with the arrival of 14,000 National Guard troops. In the end, the Watts Rebellion left 34 dead, 1,032 injured, nearly 4,000 arrested and $40 million dollars in property damage.
Patsy Takemoto Mink, third-generation Japanese American and Democrat, is elected to represent Hawai’i. She is the first woman of color elected to U.S. Congress.

Malcolm X is assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom in New York City. Exactly who was responsible for the assassination remains a mystery, largely because the NY Police Department refuses to disclose its surveillance files from that time period.

President Johnson declares a War on Crime in a Special Message on Law Enforcement to Congress, saying, “No right is more elemental to our society than the right to personal security and no right needs more urgent protection... We must arrest and reverse the trend toward lawlessness." This leads to the creation of the Law Enforcement Assistance Act, creating a direct role for the federal government in local policing, court systems, and state prisons, often providing military-grade weapons, gear, and training to local police departments.

600 Alabama civil rights activists stage a Selma-to-Montgomery protest march to draw attention to the continued denial of black voting rights. The marchers are confronted by Alabama State Troopers, whose attack on them at the Edmund Pettus Bridge is carried on national television. Two weeks later, Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. leads a five-day, 54-mile march, retracing the route of the original activists. The 3,300 marchers at the beginning of the trek eventually grow to 25,000 when they reach the Alabama capitol on March 25. After the march, Pres. Lyndon Johnson proposes the Voting Rights Act to guarantee black voting throughout the South.

The White House releases "The Negro Family: The Case For National Action," also known as the Moynihan Report. It claims that “at the heart of the deterioration of the fabric of Negro society is the deterioration of the Negro family”—which it blames on black matriarchy. The report proceeds to encourage black military service, hailing the U.S. armed forces as “an utterly masculine world” that is “a dramatic and desperately needed change: a world away from women, a world run by strong men of unquestioned authority.”
The Voting Rights Act. A landmark piece of federal legislation aimed at local and state barriers for black people voting prohibits racial discrimination in voting.

In California, the mostly Filipino members of the Agricultural Workers’ Organizing Committee convene at Delano’s Filipino Community Hall and vote to go on strike against Delano’s table grape growers. The Delano Grape Strike is led by Larry Itliong, who had formed AWOC in 1959 along with fellow Filipino labor leaders Philip Vera Cruz and Pete Velasco. Itliong asks the National Farm Workers Association, led by Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta, to join the strike. The following year, the two unions merge and become the United Farm Workers, with Chavez as director and Itliong as assistant director. The UFW would become the largest and most important farm worker union in the nation.

The Hart-Celler Act, intended to purge racial restrictions in immigration law, particularly against Asians, Africans, and southern and eastern Europeans, abolishes the national origins quota system and replaces it with a new system that prioritizes family reunification and professional migration. It leads to a dramatic rise in authorized immigrants from Asia and also dramatically increases unauthorized immigration from Latin America, since previously there had been no numerical limits on immigration in the Western Hemisphere, including Latin America or the Caribbean.

U.S. President Lyndon Johnson deploys American combat troops to Vietnam, massive escalation of U.S. military effort. Anti war demonstrations become widespread, with nightly TV coverage of war and opposition of liberal news media.
At least 43,000 Indigenous Americans fight in the Vietnam War.
Black Panther Party forms in Oakland, California.

In Seattle, approximately 3,000 students, including about 1,000 white and Asian-American students, boycott their regular classes to attend eight Freedom Schools in churches and community buildings throughout the Central District. There, students in integrated settings take courses on African-American history and civil rights taught by volunteer teachers, including many college students on spring break. Three public school teachers also instruct students during the boycott.  The surprising support for the boycott forced the Seattle School Board to eventually implement most of the programs requested by boycott leaders.

New York Times publishes William Peterson’s “Success Story: Japanese American Style.” US News and World Report publishes “Success Story of One Minority Group in US,” praising Chinese Americans and Chinatowns.

Dr. King's speech, "Beyond Vietnam: A Time to Break Silence," generates much criticism from both white and black media outlets urging him to stick to the topic of Civil Rights. After describing the history of U.S. involvement with Vietnam, Dr. King blames increasing military spending for draining resources from domestic programs meant to fight poverty and racism, thereby drawing a direct connection between the "evil triplets" of racism, materialism, and militarism. He proclaims that young black men, "crippled by our society," were being sent "eight thousand miles away to guarantee liberties in Southeast Asia which they have not found in southwest Georgia and East Harlem."

Beginning in April, 159 urban uprisings erupt across the United States. The first occurred in Cleveland, but by far the most devastating take place in Newark, New Jersey, and Detroit, Michigan. The former takes 26 lives and injures 1,500; the latter results in 40 deaths and 2,000 injuries.
Thurgood Marshall becomes the first black justice on the U.S. Supreme Court.
Loving v. Virginia. In a landmark civil rights decision, the Supreme Court invalidates laws prohibiting interracial marriage.

The 1967 War between Palestinians and Israel was a key turning point that would prefigure subsequent decades of conflict and negotiations. During six days of war, Israel routed Egyptian, Syrian and Jordanian forces and established itself as the region’s unparalleled power, laying claim to East Jerusalem, the West Bank, Gaza, Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, and Syria’s Golan Heights. The war was dubbed by Palestinians as the Naksa, or “Setback.”

Indian Civil Rights Act (ICRA) revises Public Law 280 by requiring states to have tribal consent before extending any legal jurisdiction over an Indian reservation. It also grants most protections of the Bill of Rights and the 14th Amendment to tribal members in dealings with tribal governments. ICRA also amendsthe Major Crimes Act to include assault resulting in serious bodily harm.

The American Indian Movement (AIM) forms. Shortly after the Minneapolis Anishinaabeg formed an “Indian Patrol” to monitor police activities in Indian neighborhoods, Dennis Banks forms AIM, comprised mainly of urban Indigenous youth who believe that direct and militant confrontation with the U.S. government is the only way to redress historical grievances and to gain contemporary civil rights; and that the tribal governments organized under the IRA (1934) are not legitimate or grounded in traditional Indian ways.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee. In the wake of the assassination, 125 cities in 29 states experience uprisings. Over a week, 46 people are killed and 35,000 are injured in these confrontations. Some of the biggest uprisings are in Washington, D.C., Baltimore, Chicago, and Kansas City.
Civil Rights Act outlaws discrimination in housing rental and sales.

The Poor People’s Campaign, led by SCLC, moves forward, despite King’s assassination. The campaign addresses issues affecting all poor people regardless of race, aiming to secure federal legislation for full employment and the construction of low-income housing. Protestors who gathered in Washington, D.C., are from a wide range of racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic backgrounds: Native Americans, Latinos, poor whites, and rural and urban blacks. However, the number of protestors fell far short of the goal of 50,000 people.
Sen. Robert F. Kennedy, a presidential candidate and supporter of the Poor People’s Campaign, is assassinated in Los Angeles.

Shirley Chisholm of New York becomes the first black woman elected to Congress. She unsuccessfully runs for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972, the same year that Barbara Jordan becomes one of two black Congress members to be elected from the South for the first time since 1898.

My Lai Massacre. U.S. soldiers of Charlie Company of the 11th Infantry Brigade arrive at the village of My Lai in South Vietnam while on a “search and destroy” mission to root out the 48th Viet Cong Battalion. The unit meets no resistance from the 700 inhabitants yet kill as many as 504 Vietnamese civilians including 119 children 7 years old and younger, and 27 in their 70s or 80s.

Milton Meyer Company, owner of the International Hotel in San Francisco’s Manilatown, applies to demolish the building, mobilizing Asian-American activists to prevent the eviction of its elderly Asian residents.
Students with the Third World Liberation Front at San Francisco State begin a five-month strike for a College of Ethnic Studies and other reforms.

“Indians of All Tribes” occupation of Alcatraz. A group of young Indians seize the abandoned Alcatraz Island in San Francisco harbor and issue a “Proclamation to the Great White Father” claiming that Alcatraz is suitable as an Indian Reservation and thus, should be converted into an Indian educational and cultural center. The Indians of All Tribes continue to occupy Alcatraz until 1971.
Black Panthers Fred Hampton, 21, and Mark Clark, 22, are gunned down by 14 police officers as they lie sleeping in their Chicago, Illinois, apartment.
Kevin Phillips publishes The Emerging Republican Majority, arguing that racial resentments was fueling a historical political realignment that would cement a new Republican majority for decades.

Primarily middle-aged, middle-class Japanese, Chinese, and Filipinos, including pastors and medical doctors, form the Asian Coalition for Equality (ACE) in Seattle, which vociferously speaks out against police brutality and racism and actively supports African American campaigns.

Asian Americans for Action (Triple A), NYC. Multi-generational, anti-imperialist group whose leadership consists mostly of middle-aged Japanese American/Nisei women is formed.  The demonstrate against the Vietnam War, U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, community control of schools, and organized study groups and educational forums. Precursor to the revolutionary collective I Wor Kuen.

Faced with slum housing, inadequate schools and rising unemployment, Puerto Rican youth in Chicago form the Young Lords Organization, inspired in part by the writings of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. An outgrowth of the Young Lords street gang, the YLO becomes a vibrant community organization, creating free breakfast programs for kids and community health clinics. Modeled after the Black Panthers, the YLO uses direct action and political education to bring public attention to issues affecting their community. The group later spreads to New York City.
Pres. Richard Nixon signs Public Law 91-550, the first restitution of land to any Indigenous nation, restoring 48,000 acres of the sacred Blue Lake to the Taos Pueblo nation.

San Rafael, California, courthouse shooting results in the death of Judge Harold Haley and 3 others. UCLA Philosophy Professor Angela Davis is implicated in the shooting and becomes the subject of a nationwide FBI-led search. Davis is captured and brought to trial. She is acquitted of all charges in 1972.
Kent State Massacre. Four white Kent State University students are killed and several more injured when members of the Ohio National Guard open fire during a demonstration protesting the Vietnam War.

At least 37 prison uprisings erupt around the country, the bloodiest and most infamous of which takes place at Attica Correctional Facility in upstate New York. In September, unarmed inmates seize control of the Attica prison. The four-day rebellion was prompted by long-standing complaints about overcrowding, abysmal conditions, and systematic racism by prison guards. Several officers are taken hostage. Negotiations between the inmates and the authorities fail, and state troopers storm the prison, shooting indiscriminately. They kill at least 39 people, including 29 prisoners and 9 guards. Many others are injured.

The Powell Memo. A confidential memo for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, drafted by Lewis F. Powell Jr. as a roadmap to defend and advance free enterprise against perceived socialist, communist, and fascist momentum, calls for new think tanks to produce research and influence politics and universities in support of free market economics, the takeover of both political parties, large tax cuts, deregulation and privatization, legal strategies such as winning the treatment of campaign contributions as free speech, media strategies, free trade agreements, and more. The memo is believed to have led to the formation of several influential conservative think tanks and lobbying organizations like the Business Roundtable, the Heritage Foundation, and the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), which in turn gave rise to influential conservative intellectualism and philanthropy that deeply shaped public opinion.

Anti-Imperialist Women's Conference, Vancouver, Canada. Six women from North and South Vietnam and Laos meet with 200 women from North America in an effort to end the war and is attended by many Asian-American women and vets.

Winter Soldier Investigation, Detroit. Sponsored by Vietnam Veterans Against the War, testimonies by veterans about atrocities they witnessed and took part in during Southeast Asian War include 2 Asian-American veterans who speak about the racism they endured from fellow soldiers.

Trail of Broken Treaties. Over 500 Indigenous activists travel to Washington, D.C., with plans to deliver a 20-point proposal to revamp the BIA and establish a government commission to review treaty violations. When guards at the BIA inform the tribal members that Bureau officials would not meet with them and threaten forcible removal from the premises, the activists begin a weeklong siege of the building. The BIA finally agrees to review the demands and to provide funds to transport the activists back home. Shortly thereafter, the FBI classifies AIM as “an extremist organization” and adds its leaders to the list of “key extremists” in the U.S.

Indian Education Act establishes funding for special bilingual and bicultural programs, culturally relevant teaching materials, and appropriate training and hiring of counselors. It also creates an Office of Indian Education in the U.S. Department of Education.
CBS’s 60 Minutes broadcasts “100% Americans,” a feature highlighting the assimilation and mobility of Japanese Americans. Host Mike Wallace describes them as “the model minority.”

Gov. Nelson Rockefeller enacts the Rockefeller Drug Laws, mandating extremely harsh prison terms for possession or sale of relatively small amounts of drugs. Although claiming to target “kingpins,” most people incarcerated under the laws are convicted of low-level, nonviolent, first-time offenses. The laws mark an unprecedented shift towards addressing drug use and abuse through the criminal justice system instead of through the medical and public health systems. New York’s Rockefeller Drug Laws would become the national policy model for the drug war; throughout the 1970s, other states followed and enacted their own versions of the Rockefeller Drug Laws, as did Congress in the 1980s. These policies were driven not by evidence but largely by politicians and special interest groups with a stake in appearing “tough on crime.”

Wounded Knee Occupation. At the Pine Ridge Reservation of the Oglala Sioux in South Dakota, trouble had been brewing between the Indian activists that supported AIM, and tribal leaders who had the support of the BIA. After a violent confrontation, tribal chair Richard Wilson condemns AIM and bans it from the reservation. AIM leaders, led by Russell Means, and about 200 activists, who are supported by some Oglala traditional leaders, take over the village of Wounded Knee, announce the creation of the Oglala Sioux Nation, declare themselves independent from the United States, and define their national boundaries as those determined by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. The siege lasts 71 days. Federal marshals, FBI agents, and armored vehicles surround the village. AIM members agree to end their occupation on the condition that the government convene a full investigation into their demands and grievances.

National Black Feminist Organization is established, with founding members including Florynce Kennedy, Michele Wallace, Faith Ringgold, Doris Wright, and Margaret Sloan-Hunter. Founders address issues affecting black women, which they felt were ignored both in the white female-dominated feminist movement and in the male-dominated Civil Rights and Black Power movement. The first regional conference in New York City attracts 400 women and establishes 10 chapters nationwide.
The United States and North Vietnam sign a ceasefire agreement.

United States v. Washington. “Boldt decision” reaffirms the reserved right of American Indian tribes in the State of Washington to act alongside the state as co-managers of salmon and other fish and to continue harvesting them in accordance with the treaties that the United States signed with the tribes.

Jung Sai Garment Workers' Strike, San Francisco. Representative of the post-1965 wave of Chinese workers, a successful yearlong strike that includes 64 arrests shows the strength of labor activism among immigrant workers facing unfair labor practices. With the slogan, “If you’re not afraid, join us. If you are afraid, this isn’t the place for you,” the strike transforms the workers and the Chinatown community itself, dispelling stereotypes of Chinese immigrant women. As the San Francisco Chronicle noted, “Any warmed-over stereotypes about Oriental impassiveness were convincingly shot down yesterday.”

Combahee River Collective. Founded by black feminists and lesbians in Boston, Massachusetts, the collective is best known for its Combahee River Collective Statement, which addressed the intersection of multiple oppressions, including racism and heterosexism. The Collective’s name refers to Harriet Tubman’s military campaign in 1863 in South Carolina, the Combahee River Raid, which freed more that 750 slaves.
President Nixon resigns.

Lau v. Nichols. U.S. Supreme Court reaffirms the 1970 memorandum, ruling students' access to, or participation in, an educational program cannot be denied because of their inability to speak or understand English. The lawsuit had begun as a class action by Chinese-speaking students against the school district in San Francisco. Congress passes the Equal Educational Opportunity Act of 1974 to make bilingual education more widely available in public schools.

Pine Ridge Reservation Shootout. Two FBI agents enter the Pine Ridge Reservation supposedly looking for a tribal member on theft and assault charges. Shots are fired under confusing circumstances, resulting in the death of the agents and one AIM member. The violence that ensues is coupled with the criminalization of the AIM movement and results in an undermining of the Indian movement for self-determination. AIM activist Leonard Peltier is arrested, tried, and convicted for the deaths, and sentenced to double life imprisonment.

Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act recognizes U.S. obligation to provide for maximum participation by Indigenous people in Federal services to and programs in their communities, establishes a goal to provide education and services for Indian children, and declares a commitment to maintain the U.S. government's continuing trust relationship, and responsibility to, individual Indians and tribes.
Leaders from over 20 tribes form the Council of Energy Resource Tribes (CERT) to help secure better terms from corporations seeking to exploit valuable mineral resources on reservations.

Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, falls to North Vietnamese forces. After a 5-year civil war in Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge captures the capital city of Phnom Penh. The United States authorizes the entry of 130,000 evacuees from Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos (the “first wave”) and makes plans for their settlement in the United States through the Indochina Migration and Refugee Assistance Act.

Church Committee is established to investigate widespread intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA. Over 9 months, the committee interviewed over 800 officials, held 250 executive and 21 public hearings. Among matters investigated are attempts to assassinate foreign leaders, including Patrice Lumumba of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rafael Trujillo of the Dominican Republic, the Diem brothers of Vietnam, Gen. René Schneider of Chile, and a plan to use the Sicilian Mafia to kill Fidel Castro of Cuba.

After non-English speakers testify about the discrimination they face at the polls, Congress votes to expand the U.S. Voting Rights Act to require language assistance at polling stations. Native Americans, Asian Americans, Alaska Natives, and Latinos benefit most from this provision. (The original Act, passed in 1965, had applied only to Blacks and Puerto Ricans.)
Residents of the International Hotel are evicted after a nearly decade-long standoff.

Indian Child Welfare Act. In response to the widespread practice of transferring the care and custody of Indian children to non-Indians, the act recognizes the authority of tribal courts to hear the adoption and guardianship cases of Indian children and establishes a strict set of statutory guidelines for those cases heard in state court.

American Indian Religious Freedom Act promises to “protect and preserve for American Indians their inherent right of freedom to believe, express, and exercise” traditional religions, “including but not limited to access to sites, use and possession of sacred objects, and the freedom to worship through ceremonial and traditional rites.” The Act contains no enforcement provisions.

Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe. U.S. Supreme Court rules that Indian tribal courts do not have inherent criminal jurisdiction to try and to punish non-Indians, and cannot assume such jurisdiction unless specifically authorized to do so by Congress. The decision states that tribal powers could be divested both explicitly and implicitly, if they are in violation of their status of “domestic dependent nations.”

Santa Clara v. Martinez. U.S. Supreme Court Decision severely limits the effects of the Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 by ruling that Indian tribes are “distinct, independent political communities retaining their original natural rights in matters of self-government.” Suits against the tribe under ICRA are barred by the tribe's sovereign immunity.
Federal Acknowledgment Project establishes the Branch of Acknowledgment and Research within the BIA to evaluate the claims of non-recognized Indian tribes for Federal acknowledgement.
The Seminoles become the first tribe to enter into the bingo gaming industry, encouraging other tribes to begin gaming enterprises on reservations as a step towards greater economic self-sufficiency.
United States establishes diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China and reunites members of long-separated Chinese-American families.

The United Nations establishes the Orderly Departure Program (ODP) to deal with the “second wave” of refugees from Southeast Asia. The United States quickly becomes the largest country of second asylum. Racial tensions between recent Vietnamese arrivals and white residents in Seadrift, Texas, escalates when a group of Vietnamese fishermen are accused of murdering a white American.

United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians. U.S. Supreme Court rules that the Sioux are entitled to $17.5 million plus 5% interest per year since 1877, totaling about $106 million, in compensation for the unjust taking of the Black Hills and in direct contravention of the Treaty of Fort Laramie. The Great Sioux Nation refuses to take the money, which still sits in a trust fund in Washington, collecting interest, instead demanding that its treaty lands be returned.

Congress passes the Refugee Act, the first to explicitly deal with refugees apart from other immigration categories. It creates a comprehensive system for the admission of refugees and significantly slows entry from Southeast Asia.
The Mariel boatlift transports 125,000 Cubans to Florida, including a large number of Afro-Cubans.

ranges.Event: The U.S. Immigration Service arrests and deports more than 3.8 million Latin Americans under "Operation Wetback." Many U.S. citizens, including political activist Luisa Moreno and other community leaders, are deported unfairly.

Corporate expansion in Hawai'i not only assaults urban enclaves of Chinatown and Little Tokyo but also invades rural valleys. The first mass eviction takes place in 1970 in Kalama Valley, where small farmers were uprooted for a housing development. Kalama Valley is sacrificed, but the struggle provides experience and indignation to spur more people to fight the onslaught of other evictions.

A U.S.-backed military coup led by Augusto Pinochet overthrows Salvador Allende's socialist government, barely three years after Allende was elected. Pinochet outlaws political parties and criminalizes leftists as "domestic enemies." Violence and "disappearances" are frequent. When Pinochet's attempts at economic restructuring fail, a group of Chicago School economists (taught by Milton Friedman) advocate a drastic free-market approach. The government slashes welfare programs, liberalizes trade, and deregulates the financial sector, which leads to mass unemployment, loss of purchasing power, and extreme inequality.

Thatcherism, the social and economic policy and political style of the British Conservative Party under Margaret Thatcher's leadership. As Prime Minister, she erodes the power of the trade unions and privatized state-owned industries. Most famously, she blames the stagnant and declining economic condtions of the British working and middle classes on the changing racial demographics of England.

years.Event: Ronald Reagan is elected President of the United States. Building on the Southern Strategy, he launches his campaign in Neshoba County, Mississippi, the site of the murders of 3 civil rights workers in 1964, declaring, “I believe in states' rights.”

Seminole Tribe v. Butterworth. U.S. Supreme Court Decision rules that tribes have the right to create gambling enterprises on their land, even if civil statutes of the state prohibit them. The ruling allows reservations to establish casinos and gives reservations greater authority for tribal governments to levy taxes, own assets, and create judiciaries.

May Chen, of the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union, leads New York Chinatown strike of 1982, one of the largest Asian-American worker strikes, with about 20,000 garment factory workers marching the streets of Lower Manhattan demanding work contracts.

Indian Mineral Development Act. Indian tribes are declared to have flexibility in developing and selling mineral resources, including joint venture agreements with mineral developers. The act aims to further the policy of self-determination and to maximize financial return to tribes.
Ronald Ebens and Michael Nitz beat Chinese American Vincent Chin to death with a baseball bat in Detroit, blaming “Japs” for the loss of Detroit auto industry jobs.
Pres. Ronald Reagan signs a law making January 20 a federal holiday in honor of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Congress approves the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA), providing legalization for certain undocumented workers, including agricultural workers. The Act also creates employer sanctions, making it illegal for employers to hire undocumented workers.

The Black-Korean Alliance (BKA) is established in response to tensions between the two communities in Los Angeles. It would disband in 1992, with co-chair Bong Hwan Kim saying, “We recognized that dialogue alone wouldn't be enough. We have to look at the economic problems that create tensions.”
California v. Cabazon. U.S. Supreme Court Decision finds that states permitting any form of gambling cannot prohibit Indians from operating gambling facilities.
HR 442. The Civil Liberties Act of 1987 is passed and becomes law the following year. Among its provisions is restitution to survivors of Japanese-American mass incarceration during WWII.
A retrial for the killing of Vincent Chin finds Ronald Ebens innocent on all counts, prompting outrage and organizing among Asian Americans. An earlier civil rights trial had acquitted Nitz.
Indian Gaming Regulatory Act affirms the right of tribes to conduct gaming on Indian lands but makes it subject to tribal/state compact negotiations for certain gaming.

Led by university students, over 1 million Chinese in Tiananmen Square demand reforms by the Chinese Communist government. In 1992, the U.S. passes the Chinese Student Protection Act, giving all PRC citizens in the U.S. between June 1989 and April 1990 permission to apply for permanent residency.
President George H. W. Bush signs into law an entitlement program to pay each surviving Japanese-American internee $20,000.

Native American Languages Act makes it U.S. policy to “preserve, protect, and promote the rights and freedom of Native Americans to use, practice, and develop Native American languages.” By 2017, many American Indian languages would be lost and fewer than 100 languages would be spoken by Indians.

Native American Grave Protection and Repatriation Act requires all institutions that receive federal funds to inventory their collections of Indian human remains and artifacts, make their lists available to Indian tribes, and return any items requested by the tribes.

Indigenous Environmental Network forms from a national gathering of tribal grassroots youth and Indigenous leadership addressing common experiences of environmental assaults on a number of tribal communities and villages through large toxic municipal and hazardous waste dumps and nuclear waste storage facilities, and industrial and mineral development.

Black protestors organize a boycott of the Korean-owned Family Red Apple Market in Flatbush, New York, following an altercation between a black customer and the proprietor in which the former was suspected of shoplifting.

Iraq invades Kuwait. Fearing the loss of control over oil in the Middle East, U.S. and allied forces attacked Iraq. Some estimate up to 35,000 Iraqi solders are killed, compared to 146 U.S. soldiers. Afterward, Pres. George H. W. Bush declares before the corporate-funded American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), “By God, we've kicked the Vietnam syndrome once and for all.” Between 1990 and 1997, there would be over 30 U.S. military interventions.

Kim Hak-sun publicly tells her story as a former ianfu. From 1932 to 1945, the Japanese Imperial Army forced between 80,000 and 200,000 women and girls into sexual slavery, calling them ianfu, or "comfort women"—a euphemism for sex slave—for the military. Most women were from occupied Korea, but many also came from other Japanese-occupied territories in China, the Philipines, and Indonesia. After Kim Hak-sun's testimony, three former sex slaves file a class action suit against the Japanese government demanding compensation and an apology. To this day, there has never been a fair and adequate response to the ongoing demands by surviving comfort women for justice.

U.S. president George H. W. Bush transforms part of Gantanamo into an indefinite detetion center for HIV-positive Haitian refugees, called Camp Bulkeley. Located in southern Cuba, the bay was named Guantanamo by its Indigenous inhabitants, the Taínos. The United States had seized control of Guantano Bay in a bid for overseas territorial powers after the Spanish–American War of 1898 and had used it as an active military base ever since, making it the oldest overseas U.S. military encampment. The U.S. would call the camp a humanitarian endeavor. It would woulater be transformed into an indefinite detention and torture site for so-called "enemy combatants" during the War on Terror.

Black teenager Latasha Harlins is shot and killed by Empire Liquor Market proprietor Soon Ja Du following an altercation between the two. Although Du is found guilty of manslaughter, she receives probation, a small fine, and community service.
Los Angeles riots erupt on April 29, following the acquittal of Los Angeles police officers in the beating of black motorist Rodney King. Korean-owned businesses are targeted.

Religious Freedom Restoration Act states that state governments “shall not substantially burden a person's exercise of religion” except if such exercise of religion conflicts with “a compelling government interest.” In 1997, the Supreme Court declares this unconstitutional as applied to the states.
President Clinton signs into law the largest federal crime bill in U.S. history with sweeping provisions, including massive expansion of death penalty crimes and prison construction.

The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) is signed on January 1 between Mexico, Canada, and the United States. The agreement eliminates most tariffs and other regulations viewed as "trade barriers" between these nations, promising to increase prosperity and cooperation. NAFTA would fail to deliver on this promise, as corporations and capital become free to move to places with the lowest wages and regulations, and workers suffer as a result. Mexico experiences the loss of 2 million agricultural jobs as small farmers are forced to compete with highly subsidized U.S. exports such as corn, which drives migration to the United States. While manufacturings jobs increase in Mexico, they decline in the United States. Wages and worker protections everywhere stagnate or decline, falling far short of the promised growth of the middle class and instead distributing wealth and political power upward.
California voters pass Proposition 184, known as “three strikes, you’re out”—the nation’s toughest mandatory sentencing law.
California voters pass Proposition 187, denying undocumented immigrants public services like education and healthcare.
Operation Gatekeeper marks massive increase in U.S. Border Patrol spending, militarizing the U.S.-Mexico border.

Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols carry out the bombing of a federal building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring more than 500. McVeigh had rightwing ideological roots in the Patriot and Neo-Nazi movements.
President Clinton declares November of each year to be National American Indian Heritage Month.

President Clinton signs a bill that ends AFDC and replaces it with Temporary Assistance to Needy Families (TANF). Before he was elected president in 1992, Bill Clinton ran on a platform of “ending welfare as we know it.” At the time, a New Deal-era program called Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) provided payments to children whose parents were unemployed, deceased, disabled, or absent from the household. States administered AFDC and were entitled to unlimited matching funds from the federal government. Critics of AFDC charged that the program was too costly, discouraged parents from finding work, and encouraged unmarried women to have children. The new program places limits on federal welfare spending, prevented parents from receiving funds for more than 5 years in a lifetime and mandated that recipients enroll in job training “workfare” programs. Clinton’s welfare reform effort was immediately controversial for the potential hardships it posed to low-income Americans. Several high-level officials at the Department of Health and Human Services resign in protest of the new law.

California voters approve Proposition 209, ending the use of affirmative action in public higher education, employment, and contracting. Two years later, Washington State voters would approve a similar measure.

Congress passes the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRAIRA), and the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA), which deeply alter the legal landscape for immigrants and refugees. Among the sweeping changes, the laws create new forms of punishment like mandatory detention; vastly expand the definition of “aggravated felony” under immigration law, making people deportable for crimes that carry sentences of one year or more; apply new criminal deportation provisions retroactively; and eliminate judicial review in criminal deportation cases. Deportation and immigration detention skyrockets.

Shawn Berry, Lawrence Russell Brewer, and John King murder a 49-year-old black man, James Byrd Jr. by dragging him for three miles behind a pick-up truck, which severs his arm and head, and dump his torso in front of a black cemetery in Jasper, Texas.
Shannon County, South Dakota, home of the Oglala Lakota on Pine Ridge Reservation, is identified as the poorest place in the country.
In the Bronx, plainclothes NYPD officers shoot at 23-year-old unarmed Guinean immigrant Amadou Dialo 41 times, killing him. The officers are later acquitted of all charges.

Taiwanese-American scientist Wen Ho Lee is arrested on suspicion of spying for China and placed in solitary confinement. Based on lack of any evidence of espionage, the government would later drop 58 of its 59 charges against Lee.

WTO protests in Seattle. A series of protests against the World Trade Organization, a world meeting of international organizations associated with economic globalization. With 40,000 protesters, it dwarfs any previous U.S. demonstration against a world meeting on globalization.
Koch Industries agrees to pay a $35 million fine due to a series of oil pipeline leaks, including 300 from 1990 to 1997.
In a dramatic reversal of past policy, the AFL-CIO calls for an immediate amnesty for undocumented immigrants and an end to employer sanctions.

California voters pass Proposition 21, which expands criminal punishments of youth offenders, expands the definition of gang affiliation, and allows children as young as 14 to be prosecuted as adults.

The U.S. prison population reaches 2 million. This total represents persons held in federal and state prisons, territorial prisons, local jails, immigration facilities, military prisons, jails on Indian reservations, and juvenile facilities.
Four days of civil unrest follow the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Black male, Timothy Thomas, by white police officer Steven Roach in Cincinnati.

On Sept. 11, 2001, al-Qaeda militants carry out attacks the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon just outside of Washington, D.C. Commonly referred to as 9/11, the attacks trigger a major U.S. domestic and global military, political, legal, and conceptual framework launched by Pres. George W. Bush under the name “The War on Terror.” Although the stated goal is to combat terrorism, these policies, ideas, and rhetoric would lead to rampant profiling, surveillance, and threats to the lives of Muslims and people perceived to be Muslim.

Congress passes the sweeping USA PATRIOT Act with very little debate, vastly expanding the powers of law enforcement and ushering in a new era of racial profiling, immigrant detentions, and deportations.

Frank Roque shoots and kills Balbir Singh Sodhi on September 15, 2001, in Arizona, the first fatal act of hate violence resulting from 9/11. Mr. Sodhi was a 49-year-old Sikh-American man who owned a Chevron gas station in Mesa, Arizona. He was shot while arranging American flags in front of his gas station. His assailant, Frank Roque, wanted to "kill a Muslim" in retaliation for the terrorist attacks. He selected Mr. Sodhi simply because he had a beard and wore a turban in accordance with his Sikh faith. Mr. Roque shoots at Mr. Sodhi three times, then shoots at another service station owned by a Lebanese American, and finally at the home of a family of Afghan descent.

U.S. and Israeli delegations walk out of the World Conference against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia, and Related Intolerance over a draft resolution criticizing the state of Israel and equating Zionism with racism.

After the September 11 attacks, the George W. Bush administration uses the term "enemy combatant" to include any person with alleged ties to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or other U.S. designated "terrorist organizations." A legal term, those designated as enemy combatants could be tortured and held idefinitely without due process. The U.S. creates this category of persons to circumvent the Geneva Conventions' rules governing prisoners of war. Using this new term, the U.S. pursues torture and endless imprisonment as a governmental and military policy. In 2009, the Obama administration would stop using the term.

The National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) requires certain men and boys over 16 from 25 countries (all of which were predominantly Muslim countries from Asia and Africa, except North Korea) to report to immigration offices between November 2002 and April 2003 for fingerprinting, photographing, and interrogation or else face arrest, detention, or deportation. Registration would also often lead to arrest, detention, or deportation, mainly for minor immigration violations that would have been ignored otherwise. This creates a catch-22 and widespread uncertainty and fear. Although the U.S. government would declare the end of NSEERS in 2011, its effects continue, effectively making the religious, cultural, and political affiliations, and lawful activities of Muslims and those perceived to by Muslim the bases for justifying detention, deportation, and denial of immigration benefits.

Cambodia signs a repatriation agreement with the United States, triggering a deportation crisis in Cambodian-American communities. As a result, hundreds of refugees who fled the Khmer Rouge would be deported to Cambodia.

An estimated 10-15 million people in hundreds of cities around the world participate in coordinated protests against the imminent U.S. invasion of Iraq. By several accounts, it is the largest mass protest in world history.

The Minuteman Project begins, organizing organize anti-immigrant activists at the U.S./Mexico border. The group considers itself a citizen's border patrol, but several known white supremacists are members. During the next two years, the Minuteman Project would gain widespread press coverage. Immigrant rights supporters conduct counter-rallies in public opposition to the Minuteman Project's tactics and beliefs.

Hurricane Katrina, the strongest hurricane ever recorded in the Gulf of Mexico, devastates New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, killing 1,800 people and displacing 600,000 households. A Category 5 hurricane with winds of 175 miles per hour, its record would be broken a few weeks later by Hurricane Rita. 40,000 National Guard troops are deployed, yet the poor and working-class Blacks shoulder the burden of the storm's devastation, highlighting decades of poverty, segregation, and deep disenfranchisement.

Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS), a Palestinian-led movement for freedom, justice and equality. It urges nonviolent pressure on Israel until it complies with international law by meeting three demands: ending its occupation and colonization of all Arab lands and dismantling the Wall; recognizing the fundamental rights of the Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel to full equality; and respecting, protecting, and promoting the rights of Palestinian refugees to return to their homes and properties as stipulated in UN Resolution 194.

Blackwater, a private military contractor, is founded by Erik Prince (brother of current U.S. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos). A squad of armed Blackwater contractors kills 17 Iraqi civilians and injurs 20 others at Nisour traffic circle in Baghdad, setting off several investigations into Blackwater's conduct. Although Blackwater's image becomes deeply tainted by its disastrous operations in Iraq, it renames and rebrands itself as Academi and has continued to secure millions in contracts from the U.S. government, including a 2010 contract with the CIA for $250 million. Academi would become part of a merged group of private security companies, Constellis Holdings, Inc.

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) is adopted by the UN General Assembly by a majority of 144 states in favor, 4 votes against (Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States), and 11 abstentions (Azerbaijan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Burundi, Colombia, Georgia, Kenya, Nigeria, Russian Federation, Samoa and Ukraine).
Barack Obama becomes the first black president of the United States.

Arizona passes SB1070, requiring police to determine the immigration status of anyone arrested or detained when there is “reasonable suspicion” that they are undocumented. The law targets Latinos and leads to widespread racial profiling and copycat measures in several states.

Led by Indigenous peoples from all over the world, more than 35,000 gather for the World Peoples Conference on Climate Change and the Protection of Life in Cochabamba, Bolivia, calling for a universal declaration of the rights of Mother Earth.

The Tunisian Revolution emerges as an intensive campaign of civil resistance, leading to the ousting of longtime president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in January 2011, and eventually to a thorough democratization of the country. This kicked off what became known as the "Arab Spring," a revolutionary wave of both violent and non-violent demonstrations, protests, riots, coups, and civil wars in North Africa and the Middle East. While the Arab Spring inspired other pro-democracy movements around the world, it also led in many cases to state collapse and protracted conflict. The Syrian Civil War is one example of this, in which more than 465,000 Syrians have been killed, more than a million injured, and over 12 million (half the country's prewar population) displaced from their homes.

Approximately one third of the congressional candidates identified with the Tea Party win their elections, including five of ten Senate races and 40 of 130 House races. With roots in Citizens for a Sound Economy, founded in 1984 by David and Charles Koch of Koch Industries, the Tea Party became a powerful force within the Republican Party, pushing an anti-tax, small government, and anti-regulation platform. The Southern Poverty Law Center reports that "the number of active hate groups in the United States topped 1,000 for the first time... as the radical right showed continued explosive growth in 2010. Several factors fueled the growth: resentment over the changing racial demographics of the country, frustration over the lagging economy, and the mainstreaming of conspiracy theories and other demonizing propaganda aimed at minorities and the government."

Environmental and Indigenous groups launch a massive campaign, pressing Pres. Barack Obama to reject Phase IV of the Keystone XL Pipeline project that would run through and near tribal lands, water resources, and place of spiritual significance. On Nov. 6, 2015, Obama rejects the Keystone XL Pipeline proposal.

The Occupy Movement begins in New York City's Zuccotti Park, with other Occupy protests taking place in over 951 cities across 82 countries, and over 600 communities in the United States. Protests decry the effects of globalization and neoliberalism, particularly steepening inequality, with the slogan, “We are the 99%!”

Oak Creek Massacre. 40-year-old Wade Michael Page, a white supremacist and U.S. Army veteran, fatally shoots six people and wounds four others at the Sikh temple in Oak Creek, Wisconsin, before shooting himself in the head.

George Zimmerman fatally shoots Trayvon Martin, a 17-year-old black high school student. Zimmerman, a 28-year-old mixed-race Hispanic man, is the neighborhood watch coordinator for the gated community where Martin was temporarily living and where the shooting took place.

The Association of Asian American Studies becomes the first U.S. academic association to endorse the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions campaign. The resolution states: “Whereas the Association for Asian American Studies seeks to advance a critique of U.S. empire, opposing U.S. military occupation in the Arab world and U.S. support for occupation and racist practices by the Israeli state… Be it resolved that the Association for Asian American Studies endorses and will honor the call of Palestinian civil society for a boycott of Israeli academic institutions.”

In the summer of 2104, Israel engaged the most lethal and destruction attacks on Palestine since the 1967 war. The attacks began in retaliation for the kidnapping and murder of three Israeli teenagers that Israel asserted, without proof, had been murdered by Hamas. Hostilities escalated with rocket attacks on Israel from Gaza and sustained airstrikes from Israel into Gaza. Over 2200 Palestinians were killed, most of whom (1462) were civilians. Israeli casualties included 67 soldiers and six civilians.

The fighting lasted 50 days and ended with a truce. Subsequent investigations by the UN and other international organizations found that significant war crimes were committed by both sides. Israel dismissed those findings as "biased." The extent of Palesinian civilian casualties is the focus of many Palastinian assertions of Israeli war crimes.

The Black Lives Matter movement, initiated by 3 black women organizers, Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi, takes hold, fueled by the 2013 acquittal of George Zimmerman for the killing of Trayvon Martin, the killing of Eric Garner by NYPD officers, and the killing of 18-year-old Michael Brown by a white police officer in Ferguson, Missouri.

Flint Water Crisis. To save money, Flint changes its municipal water source to the Flint River rather than the Detroit water system in the name of fiscal responsibility, creating a serious public health danger. The corrosive Flint River water causes lead from aging pipes to leach into the water supply, causing extremely elevated levels of the heavy metal. In Flint, between 6,000 and 12,000 children have been exposed to drinking water with high levels of lead, causing irreversible and permanent brain damage. The water change correlates with an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in the county that has killed 10 people and affected another 77. In 2016, the Flint Water Task Force would report, “Flint residents, who are majority black or African-American and among the most impoverished of any metropolitan area in the United States, did not enjoy the same degree of protection from environmental and health hazards as that provided to other communities.”

Ku Klux Klan leader Frazier Glenn Cross, also known as Frazier Glenn Miller, kills 3 non-Jewish people at a Jewish community center and a Jewish retirement in home in Overland Park, Kansas, the day before the start of Passover.
According to the UN, the number of people displaced by war, conflict, or persecution reaches nearly 60 million, or one in every 122 people, around the world.

During a prayer service at the Emanuel A.M.E. church in Charleston, SC, Dylan Roof, a 21-year-old white supremacist, kills nine black people including the senior pastor and state senator Clementa C. Pinckney. Upon his arrest, Roof explains that he wanted to “start a race war." A manifesto written by Roof, found after the shooting, makes clear his white supremacist beliefs, railing against Jews, Hispanics, African Americans, gays, and Muslims.

The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe sues the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers over plans to approve the Dakota Access Pipeline route under the Missouri River, alleging that the Corps failed to adequately consult tribe members before approval, and violated the National Historic Preservation Act by authorizing construction that would threaten culturally sacred sites. This kicks off a yearlong encampment of demonstrators known as Water Protectors at the Sacred Stone Camp on the Standing Rock Reservation, who suffer numerous violent clashes and severe injuries by the National Guard, the Morton County Sheriff, and private security guards hired by Energy Transfer Partners, the pipeline company. Thousands of people, representing hundreds of tribes and First Nations, join the camp from all over the world to stand in solidarity. The camp would be forcibly evacuated in February 2017.

War, violence, and persecution leaves more people around the world displaced (over 65 million) than at any time in the 70-year history of the UN High Commission on Refugees. The conflict in Syria, now in its seventh year, is the world’s biggest producer of refugees (5.5 million). Together with Afghanistan and South Sudan, this accounts for 55% of the world's refugee population.

Real estate mogul and reality-TV personality Donald Trump becomes the GOP presidential frontrunner, using racist, misogynistic, and xenophobic rhetoric and positions against illegal immigration, various free-trade agreements, and most military interventions to earn support among a base of largely white voters. His campaign has the support of hard-right constituencies like the Patriot Movement and the KKK as well as Christian Evangelicals.

Inspired by the international attention built by the Movement for Black Lives to the disproportionate number of black people killed by the police, the Guardian launches “The Counted,” a project to count the number of people killed by police and other law enforcement agencies in the United States throughout 2015 and 2016, to monitor their demographics, and to tell the stories of how they died. It finds that in 2016, Native Americans were killed by police at the highest rate, followed by black people, Latinos, Whites, and Asians and Pacific Islanders.
The wealthiest eight people in the world own as much as the poorest 3.5 billion people combined.

Donald Trump becomes the 45th president of the United States, winning the Electoral College but losing the popular vote to democrat Hillary Clinton by a margin of nearly 2.9 million. Mike Pence, a Christian Evangelical theocrat becomes Vice President. Trump fills his cabinet with figures from all sectors of the political right, including white nationalist Steve Bannon as Chief Strategist;  former Exxon Mobil CEO Rex Tillerson as Secretary of State; former senior executive at Goldman Sachs Steven Mnuchin as Secretary of the Treasury; civil rights opponent Jeff Sessions as Attorney General; proponent of privatizing Medicare Tom Price as Secretary of Health and Human Services; charter schools proponent Betsy DeVos as Secretary of Education; climate change denier Scott Pruitt as the head of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA); opponent of tribal sovereignty Ryan Zinke as Secretary of the Interior; and government surveillance zealot Mike Pompeo as head of the CIA.

As a result of the elections, the Republican Party wins control of all three branches of the federal government (Congress, the Presidency, and the Supreme Court) and 32 state legislatures (including 25 states with Republican governors). Both the Republican and Democratic parties face internal crises, with reactionary rightwing forces gaining momentum and power in the GOP and insurgent leftwing forces in the Democratic Party.

In January President Trump issues Executive Order 13769, titled Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States, commonly known as the Muslim ban. It prohibits entry for 90 days by citizens from Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen. The order also indefinitely halts refugees from Syria. Unable to surmount several legal challenges, the administration issues a second ban in March, which makes minimal changes to the first ban. Trump issues a third version of the ban in September, indefinitely banning almost all travel to the U.S. from seven countries–Iran, Libya, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Chad and North Korea. These bans violate international treaties against discrimination based on national origin, and serve to appease and further stoke anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant sentiment among Trump's base.

Weeks after the election of Trump, white supremacist leader Richard B. Spencer cries, "Hail Trump, hail our people, hail victory!" at a National Policy Institute conference, and a number of his supporters give the Nazi salute.

The day after President Trump’s inauguration, a record-breaking 4 million people protest in 600 U.S. towns and cities for a Women’s March that also inspires satellite marches around the world, from Nairobi to Beirut to Tokyo. Days later, thousands of protesters show up at several U.S. airports to protest the detention of noncitizens from seven Muslim-majority nations that Trump attempted to exclude through a travel ban.

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg denies the motion by the Standing Rock Sioux and Cheyenne River Sioux tribes for a preliminary injunction against the pipeline company, Energy Transfer Partners. A request by the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and Cheyenne River Sioux tribe for a summary judgment against the Army Corps and Dakota Access LLC, a subsidiary of the pipeline company, would remain outstanding through 2017. That request cites tribal land rights under the 1868 Ft. Laramie Treaty and argues that the Corps decision to grant the easement was "arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law." As of May 2017, the pipeline constructed thus far has leaked over 200 gallons on three separate known incidents.

One young Quinault tribal member is killed and another seriously injured at Donkey Creek near the Humptulips Campground when witnesses say the driver of a “monster” pickup truck purposely ran over them. The driver was described as white man in his mid-30s who was screaming racial slurs and war whoops when he ran over the two young people. James “Jimmy” Kramer, 20, of Taholah is killed, and Harvey Anderson, 19, of Aberdeen is hospitalized in critical condition.

Mazaska Talks campaign. Led by the 121 First Nations and Tribes, united by the Treaty Alliance Against Tar Sands Expansion and a coalition of grassroots Indigenous groups, work to win divestment from banks funding the Dakota Access Pipeline (DAPL) and all four tar sands crude-oil pipelines proposed in Canada: Keystone XL, Kinder Morgan’s TransMountain, Enbridge’s Line 3, and Energy East. As of spring 2017, over $5 billion would be withdrawn from the banks funding DAPL.

Described as one of the largest white supremacist events in recent U.S. history, the "Unite the Right" weekend of actions in Charlottesville, VA is organised by Jason Kessler, member of the Proud Boys, a white nationalist group. On Friday, marchers descend on the University of Virginia carrying torches and yelling white nationalist slogans like "White lives matter!," "Blood and soil!," “You will not replace us!,” and “Jews will not replace us!” On Saturday, heavily armed white nationalists attacked counterprotesters, eventually resulting in numerous injuries and the death of white antiracist activist Heather Heyer when white nationalist activist James Alex Fields Jr. drove his car into a crowd of counterprotesters.

Hurricane Maria rips through the Caribbean. It is the second Category 5 hurricane of the unusually active 2017 Atlantic hurricane season, causing catastrophic damage across the Northeastern Caribbean as the second most intense landfall and the costliest hurricane ever to hit the region. The hurricane completely destroys the island's power grid, leaving all 3.4 million residents without electricity. Ninety-five percent of cell networks are knocked down with 48 of the island's 78 counties networks being completely inoperable. Eighty-five percent of above-ground phone and internet cables are knocked out and only one radio station remains on-air through the storm. As of October 6, the death toll is at least 78: 30 in Dominica, 5 in the Dominican Republic, 2 in Guadeloupe, 3 in Haiti, 34 in Puerto Rico, 1 in the United States Virgin Islands, and 3 in the contiguous United States. Total losses from the hurricane are estimated at around $91 billion (2017 USD), mostly in Puerto Rico, which was already facing a crushing $74 billion debt.

The threat of renewed "hot" war on the Korean penninsula reaches a crisis point under the Trump Administration. North Korea demonstrates that its nuclear program has advanced to the point of being able to strike US territories, and threatens to strike Guam if the United States does not stop its joint military excercises with South Korea. Pres. Donald Trump, in his first address to the United Nations, derides North Korean President Kim Jong Un, calling him a “rocket man” and warning that the US may be forced to "totally destroy" North Korea (population: 25 million). Experts are increasingly alarmed by this escalation of rhetoric, noting that the US military had already killed close to 30 percent of North Korea's population through three years of intense US-led bombings during the Korean War, which never formally ended with a peace treaty.

Trump's election coincides with an upsurge in visible street protests and violence by white nationalists. In March 2017, a 28-year-old white man from Baltimore travels to New York City with the explicit aim of killing black men. He stabs 66-year-old Timothy Caughman to death and is charged with terrorism by New York state authorities. In May, a 35-year-old white man from Oregon named Jeremy Joseph Christian harasses Muslim teenagers on a train in Portland, telling them “We need Americans here!” Three white men intercede: Ricky Best, 53; Taliesin Myrddin Namkai-Meche, 23; and Micah Fletcher, 21. Christian then stabs them, killing Best and Namkai-Meche. In August, during a weekend of "Unite the Right" actions, a 20-year-old white Nazi sympathizer from Ohio speeds his car into a crowd of anti-racist protesters in Charlottesville, Virginia, killing a woman and injuring at least 19 others.

The Trump administration names “black identity extremists” as a violent threat. A report compiled by the Domestic Terrorism Analysis Unit declares: “The FBI assesses it is very likely Black Identity Extremist (BIE) perceptions of police brutality against African Americans spurred an increase in premeditated, retaliatory lethal violence against law enforcement and will very likely serve as justification for such violence.” Incidents of “alleged police abuse” have “continued to feed the resurgence in ideologically motivated, violent criminal activity within the BIE movement”. The number of police officers killed on the job remains a fraction of the number of citizens killed by officers each year, and the majority of U.S. mass shootings and domestic terrorist incidents are carried out by white men.

Democrats win decisive victories in several key elections. Ralph Northam defeats Republican Ed Gillespie in the race for governor of Virginia. Justin Fairfax and Mark Herring, Democratic nominees for lieutenant governor and attorney general, respectively, win their races in that state as well, with key issues including the economy, immigration, abortion rights, and LGBTQ rights. In New Jersey, Democratic candidate Phil Murphy defeats embattled incumbent governor Chris Christie. At least eight openly trans candidates win local elections in Virginia, Georgia, Minnesota, California, Pennsylvania, and New Hampshire.

ranges.Event: In December of 1987, 20 years into the Israeli occupation of the Gaza Strip, an Israeli truck crashes into a truck carrying Palestinian workers, killing four and injuring others. Palestinians take to the streets, throwing rocks and molotov cocktails at the heavily armed Israeli army. To the outside world, the throwing of stones becomes a powerful visual image of the first intifada, but that was just the most visible evidence of a long-built movement of non-violent resistance. Writers Shaul Mishal and Reuben Aharoni observe that “In the absence of an official and prominent local leadership, leaflets became a substitute leadership during the intifada.” Leaflets are felt everywhere, as they informed the people of where to go, what to do, and what had been achieved. Messages of upcoming strikes, boycotts, and specific campaigns make the rounds and give the people a sense of unity of purpose. The Palestinian flag and its colors are incorporated into clothing and embroidery—with restrictions on so much of their lives, Palestinians find creative ways to resist nonviolently. In 1993, secret peace talks take place, which result in the temporary removal of Israeli troops from the Gaza Strip. The ensuing Oslo peace process ultimately deflates the intifada's momentum, imposes severe restrictions on  the Palestinian people's freedom of movement and other human rights, and leads to a more explosive second intifada in 2000.

Thatcherism, the social and economic policy and political style of the British Conservative Party under Margaret Thatcher's leadership. As Prime Minister, she erodes the power of the trade unions and privatized state-owned industries. Most famously, she blames the stagnant and declining economic condtions of the British working and middle classes on the changing racial demographics of England.

Reaganism, closely linked to Thatcherism. The social and economic policy and political style of the Republican Party under the leadership of Pres. Ronald Reagan, which involves cutting government spending, attacking trade unions, reducing taxes for the rich, cutting government regulation, privatizing public-sector industries, and tightening the money supply in order to reduce inflation. Under the eight years of his presidency, the national debt almost triples and the United States goes from being the world's largest creditor-nation to the world's largest debtor. Reagan won popularity and power by appealing to the racism of white conservatives, the homophobia and sexism among Christian Evangelicals, and the profit interests of the corporate class. He also becomes renowned for cover military operations, most notably the Iran-Contra deal, in which the United States covertly supplied arms to Iran.

A U.S.-backed military coup led by Augusto Pinochet overthrows Salvador Allende's socialist government, barely three years after Allende was elected. Pinochet outlaws political parties and criminalizes leftists as "domestic enemies." Violence and "disappearances" are frequent. When Pinochet's attempts at economic restructuring fail, a group of Chicago School economists (taught by Milton Friedman) advocate a drastic free-market approach. The government slashes welfare programs, liberalizes trade, and deregulates the financial sector, which leads to mass unemployment, loss of purchasing power, and extreme inequality.

The Second Intifada, commonly known as Al-Aqsa Intifada, began in late 2000 as a result of Israeli occupation policies that violated international law and deprived Palestinians of their basic human rights. The uprising began when Israeli President, Ariel Sharon, intentionally provoked Palestinians by appearing at the Al-Aqsa mosque, the third holiest site in Islam, with more than 1,000 Israeli police shouting "the Temple Mount is in our hands!" reminding Palestinians of the 1967 Six Day War.

Palestinians immediately responded in an uprising to which the Israeli Occupation Forces reacted by launching military offensives and changing administrative rules in order to punish Palestinians. According to the Palestinian Center for Human Rights, at least 4,973 Palestinian civilians were killed during the 2nd Intifada.

Source: American Muslims for Palestine

BRICS, a group of five major, emerging, national economies: Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. All are developing or newly industrialized countries characterized by large, sometimes fast-growing economies and significant influence on regional affairs. BRICS holds yearly summits to foster the member nations' cooperation in areas including development, mutual financial assistance and support, and infrastructure.

land.title: Settler Colonialism: The drive for Land
land.content:
• Benefits capitalism through privatization of land
  • Relies on Indigenous peoples disappearing to allow for settlers’ rightful claim to land

Representative quote
"The tribes which occupied the countries now constituting the Eastern States were annihilated or have melted away to make room for the Whites. The waves of population and civilization are rolling to the westward, and we now propose to acquire the countries occupied by the red men of the South and West…"

—Pres. Andrew Jackson, 1829

labor.title: Slavery: The drive for exploitable Labor
labor.content:
• Benefits capitalism by maximizing profit and wealth for the ruling class through the treatment of people as property
  • Treats black peoples as a lower class by virtue of their race, and convinces white workers to see non-white workers as economic, cultural, and political rivals

Representative quotes
"The two great divisions of society are not the rich and the poor, but white and black, and all the former, the poor as well as the rich, belong to the upper class, and are respected and treated as equals."

—U.S. Sen. John C. Calhoun of South Carolina, 1849

"In all social systems there must be a class to do the menial duties… or you would not have that other class which leads progress… Our slaves are black, of another and inferior race… Our slaves do not vote. We give them no political power.”"

—U.S. Sen. James Henry Hammond, “Cotton Is King” speech, 1858

empire.title: Imperialism: The drive for Empire
empire.content:
• Benefits capitalism by generating profits through war and conquest
  • Asserts that non-western peoples and nations are inferior, pose a threat to western civilization, and so must be conquered

Representative quote
"Of course our whole national history had been one of expansion… [T]hat the barbarians recede or are conquered… is due solely to the power of the mighty civilized races… which by their expansion are gradually bringing peace into the red wastes where the barbarian people of the world hold sway."

—Pres. Theodore Roosevelt, following the annexation of the Philippines and Hawai’i, 1898

freedom.title: Resistance: The drive for Freedom
freedom.content:
• Fights for freedom through spontaneous uprisings and organized movements
  • Addresses contested ideas of freedom and liberation in America

Representative quote on liberatory ideas of freedom
"Even if segregation is gone, we will still need to be free; we will still have to see that everyone has a job. Even if we can all vote, but if people are still hungry, we will not be free… Singing alone is not enough; we need schools and learning… Remember, we are not fighting for the freedom of the Negro alone, but for the freedom of the human spirit, a larger freedom that encompasses all mankind."

—Ella Baker, 1964

Representative quotes on racially oppressive ideas of freedom
